segments.text: “You are under digital arrest.” It’s a scam. Here’s how these callers are traced.
First, a call about a parcel or a crime in your name. Then a video call with a fake officer and fake warrants. “Stay on camera. Tell no one. Send money to verify.”
Indian law has no “digital arrest”. Under BNSS Section 43, an arrest means actually touching or confining the person. And I4C says police, CBI, ED and judges don’t arrest on video calls.
The caller is the criminal: personating a public servant, cheating, forgery and extortion under the BNS, and Section 66D of the IT Act.
In 2024 alone: over 1.2 lakh complaints, and 1,935 crore rupees lost.
Trail one: money. It hops through layers of mule accounts, rented out or opened in someone else’s name. Investigators follow every hop through bank statements and KYC.
Speed matters. A complaint on one-nine-three-zero alerts the banks in the chain, and money still there can be put on hold.
Trail two: the phone. Call records, SIM KYC, the IMEI, and IP logs for WhatsApp calls. Police can require them under BNSS Section 94.
Many calls come from abroad, faking Indian numbers. A telecom department system now blocks such calls, and over 83,000 WhatsApp accounts used in these scams have been blocked.
The Supreme Court has ordered a CBI investigation, and asked WhatsApp and other platforms how they will stop these scams.
Got this call? Hang up. Never pay. Call one-nine-three-zero or report on cybercrime dot gov dot in. Flag the number on Chakshu, and share this with your parents.
